title: Trump Administration Ratchets Up Export Control Penalties
gist: BIS export-control fines have topped $297M as of September 2026, more than triple the prior five-year average, with more penalties approaching the statutory maximum after Biden-era rule changes removed mandatory first-offender reductions. Pending legislation could push fines higher, while voluntary self-disclosures remain the main mitigation path (99% result in no charges).

insights.claim: Higher US export-control penalties are enabled by a Biden-administration rule change that removed mandatory 25% penalty reductions for first-time offenders and raised the cap for non-egregious cases, showing bipartisan continuity in tougher enforcement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Tougher enforcement rests on cross-administration rule changes, so it is unlikely to reverse with political turnover.

insights.claim: The Export Control Reform Act of 2018 allows BIS to fine either a per-violation maximum or twice the transaction value, whichever is greater, and BIS is using aggravating factors such as acting with knowledge more aggressively to raise penalties.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Penalty exposure scales with deal size, so large dual-use transactions carry outsized tail risk.
insights.quote: BIS is also leveraging aggravating factors, such as acting with knowledge of a violation, more aggressively in order to raise penalties.
